segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Most fire-truck ladders only reached the fourth floor, which wasn't high enough.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Although laws were passed to require escape routes, many early ideas were impractical.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Like, one idea was to attach a parachute to your head.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: The parachute idea, well, this wouldn't work too well, would it?

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Other such ideas were met with resistance, too.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Enter Anna Connolly, who received patents for fire escapes in the 19th century.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Anna Connolly's initial fire escape design was a bridge, so people could safely go up to the roof or upper floors of their own building, cross to the building next door, and go down the stairs there.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: This made good sense, since most fires started on the lower floors of buildings.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: After this design Connolly created another that was a series of platforms attached to the side of a building, with ladders connecting them.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: She specified they'd be made of iron, since iron is fireproof and resists pressure.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: Well, this design worked, was practical, and was adopted across the country.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: These days buildings in the U.S. are built with interior stairwells that are fireproof for escape, and are not visible from the outside.

segments.speaker: Speaker
segments.text: But you can still see Connolly's design on older buildings in cities.
